faqs.q: How much does wildlife removal cost in Green Cove Springs?
faqs.a: In Green Cove Springs the older the house, the more the quote reflects carpentry: fitting exclusion into historic eaves and capping an unused chimney costs more than screening a modern vent. We price that honestly after inspection, separating animal removal from the custom sealing, so you can approve the whole job with eyes open.

faqs.q: Bats are roosting in my historic Green Cove Springs home — what happens next?
faqs.a: We start with identification — evening bats and Brazilian free-tailed bats are the house species in Clay County — and a count of exits at dusk. If we are inside the legal exclusion window, August 15 through April 15, we fit one-way devices, let the colony leave over several nights, then seal and clean. Between April 16 and August 14 the colony likely has flightless pups and exclusion is prohibited statewide, so summer work is inspection, sealing the unused openings, and booking the exclusion for late August.

Green Cove Springs.wildlife_intro:
Green Cove Springs wraps around its famous spring and the St. Johns River bluff, with a historic downtown of Victorian-era houses and newer subdivisions climbing the hills west of US-17. The old housing stock is the headline: raccoons and gray squirrels in the attics of century-old homes, bats in the tall rooflines near Spring Park, and roof rats — less dominant this far north, but present — in the riverfront palms. Across the river bluffs, armadillos dig the sandy yards and barred owls complain from the magnolias.

Historic-home exclusion in Green Cove Springs is carpentry as much as trapping: decorative eaves, old chimneys, and layered additions each need fitted work, and we quote it that way rather than pretending a Victorian seals like a ranch. Bat colonies in the big old houses follow the statewide season — exclusion August 15 to April 15, maternity calls in summer handled by inspection and scheduling. Work proceeds under your authorization per FWC Rule 68A-9.010, as it does everywhere in Florida.

faqs.q: How much does wildlife removal cost in Orange Park?
faqs.a: Orange Park quotes are driven by entry count under that oak canopy — a squirrel job with one chewed gable vent prices very differently from a roofline with six access points and a raccoon family in the chimney. The inspection maps them all, and the written price covers removal, sealing, and a chimney cap if the chimney is part of the story.

faqs.q: Squirrels keep getting into my Orange Park attic every fall — why?
faqs.a: Because the highway reopens. Gray squirrels here raise young in late winter and again in summer, and each new generation tests the same oak-to-roof branches and the same softened soffit corners their parents used. If the original entries were trapped but never sealed — or sealed with foam alone, which squirrels chew through in a night — the attic reads as vacant housing. Durable Orange Park work is metal-backed sealing at every corner plus branch clearance, and our squirrel service covers gray squirrels only; fox squirrels may not be taken in Florida.

Orange Park.wildlife_intro:
Orange Park is mature-suburb Clay County: 1960s-through-80s neighborhoods under heavy oak canopy along Kingsley Avenue and Blanding, Doctors Lake at its northern edge, and subdivisions that have had fifty years for wildlife to learn them. Gray squirrels are the number-one attic call, fat on acorns and bold on the rooflines; raccoons den in the big chimneys; roof rats and Norway rats both appear, the latter along the lake and creek edges. Armadillos have marched steadily into the lawns here over the past decades.

Oak management is half the squirrel answer in Orange Park — branches trimmed back from the roof change the math more than traps do — and we build that into the plan. For chimney raccoons with spring young, timing matters, and we will explain the options rather than rush. Any live trap set on your property is visited within 24 hours as Florida rule requires, and captured natives are released on site or within Clay County under the 40-acre written-permission standard.

faqs.q: Something is killing my Middleburg chickens — what do I do?
faqs.a: Start with the evidence. Raccoons reach through wire and take birds at night leaving distinctive sign; opossums kill and eat on site; a bobcat — protected from casual take in Florida except in narrow damage situations, and never euthanized if live-caught — is a different conversation entirely. We inspect the coop, read the sign, and build the fix around exclusion first: hardware cloth instead of chicken wire, buried aprons, and latched doors usually end the losses, with lawful trapping for the raccoon or opossum pressure behind it.

Middleburg.wildlife_intro:
Middleburg is Clay County's rural heart — long dirt-road lots, horse properties, mobile and site-built homes mixed along the Black Creek forks, and the Jennings State Forest at its back. Calls here are country calls: raccoons in barns and chicken coops, opossums under porches, armadillos rooting the pastures' edges, and snakes — black racers daily, cottonmouths along the creek bottoms, and the panhandle's edge species reaching down: this far north, both the timber rattlesnake and copperhead are genuine, if uncommon, possibilities in the forest fringe.

Coop and barn work comes first for many Middleburg properties; we assess the animal pressure on outbuildings as carefully as on the house. Snake identification gets extra care here because Middleburg sits where the northern venomous set overlaps the statewide one — six venomous species are theoretically possible in Clay County's north woods, though encounters concentrate on cottonmouth and pygmy. We identify from photos, remove what is lawful and safe to remove, and leave the protected eastern indigo strictly alone.

faqs.q: How much does wildlife removal cost in Fleming Island?

faqs.q: There is an alligator in our Fleming Island pond — who handles it?
faqs.a: FWC does, through its Statewide Nuisance Alligator Program, which sends contracted trappers for alligators four feet or longer that pose a threat to people, pets, or property. No private wildlife company may book that work. Report it to FWC, keep children and dogs away from the bank — most pet losses happen at dawn and dusk at the water's edge — and never feed the animal. Smaller, non-threatening gators in a pond are generally left alone by the program, and we will tell you honestly which category yours sounds like.

The landscaping is lush and so is the wildlife: raccoons in the newer attics, roof rats in the ornamental palms, armadillos digging the perfect lawns, and wading birds and an occasional alligator in the community ponds that residents ask us about weekly.

Pond alligators are the most common Fleming Island question and the answer is always referral: FWC's nuisance alligator program handles any gator of concern with its own trappers — call FWC, keep pets leashed away from pond edges, and never feed one. Our own work here is precision exclusion on newer construction: production rooflines have repeatable weak points, and sealing them properly the first time keeps the rat pressure from the preserves out of the attic for good.

faqs.q: How much does wildlife removal cost in Keystone Heights?

faqs.q: My Keystone Heights yard is full of mounds and burrows — what is what?
faqs.a: Three residents account for nearly all of it. The gopher tortoise digs one big half-moon burrow with a sandy apron — protected, hands off, 25-foot buffer. The southeastern pocket gopher makes many fan-shaped sand mounds with the hole plugged at the side — lawful to trap. The nine-banded armadillo digs shallow cone holes while feeding and a rounder burrow against a structure — also lawful work, releasable on site or within the county on 40-plus permitted acres. We sort them on site so you only pay to treat the ones that are actually pests.

Keystone Heights.wildlife_intro:
Keystone Heights is lake country at Clay County's southern tip — Lake Geneva, Brooklyn Lake, and a scatter of sand-bottom lakes among longleaf sandhills, with small-town streets and rural lots around them. The sandhill setting brings a different cast: gopher tortoises are thick in the dry sandy ground, southeastern pocket gophers mound the yards, and the houses — lake cottages, manufactured homes, older block places — host raccoons, squirrels, and the occasional skunk under a porch. Lake levels swing with drought, and wildlife shifts with them.

In Keystone Heights, tortoise literacy matters more than anywhere else in Clay County: half the 'something is digging' calls end with a protected burrow and a relieved homeowner who called before pouring a patio. We sort burrows on inspection — tortoise to referral and buffer, armadillo to trapping, pocket gopher to its own plan — and handle attic work for the lake cottages with the same care for aging roofs that the older stock requires.
